newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish court keeps couple wanted by China in jail.
newsitem.headline: Polish court keeps couple wanted by China in jail.

text.p: Poland's Supreme Court ruled on Friday against an appeal by a married couple, wanted in China for alleged financial offences, to be released from detention while they await a decision on their extradition.

PAP news agency said the court rejected a bid by Mandugeqi and his wife, Yinge, members of China's Mongolian minority, to be freed under police supervision and a promise not to leave Poland until the case is settled.

The court justified its decision by saying there was a justified suspicion that they had committed the alleged offences and that the circumstances of their departure from China confirmed fears they might try to flee, PAP reported.

The case has been taken up by Polish human rights campaigners, including the local Helsinki committee, who say that if extradited to Beijing the pair may risk execution or much harsher punishment than they would face in Poland.
In March the Warsaw appeal court overturned an earlier provincial court ruling and decided their extradition to China was legally permissible.

The couple's lawyer is seeking political asylum for them in Poland and has also lodged an appeal with the Strasbourg-based European Human Rights Commission, saying their extradition would infringe a European Human Rights Convention article banning torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment.

The Supreme Court has yet to rule on the extradition itself. Even if it allows their deportation, the prosecutor general would still be entitled to let them stay in Poland as Warsaw and Beijing do not have an extradition agreement.
The couple were held in Poland last August on the basis of an Interpol notice. Chinese authorities issued an arrest warrant in 1994, the year after they left the country.

Their lawyer Wojciech Hermelinski has said the pair face allegations of fraud, failing to repay borrowed money from banks and individuals and of not paying for goods, together involving a sum of more than $1 million.
The couple argue they have repaid practically all they owed and that Beijing is pursuing them out of political motives.
The Chinese embassy issued a statement earlier this year saying the initial court decision preventing their extradition amounted to protection of criminals.
